Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 32-year-old man with 6-week history of unilateral (left) reduced hearing accompanied by intermittent tinnitus and mild disequilibrium; plan is face-to-face otoscopic examination to rule out cerumen impaction and provide tinnitus education.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Progressive muffled hearing in left ear × 6 weeks.  
• Course: Intermittent; occasional triggers (TV/music mask ringing).  
• Associated symptoms: Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in left ear; mild “off-balance” sensation; no true vertigo, chest pain, palpitations, nausea, ear pain, discharge, pruritus, or fever.  
• Previous episode: Brief 2-day hearing difficulty ~1 year ago, resolved.  
• Past medical history / surgeries: Not discussed.  
• Medications: Not discussed.  
• Allergies: Not discussed.  
• Social / occupational / preventive: Not discussed; denies cotton-bud use.

Examination:
• Video visit only; no vitals or physical exam performed.  
• No observed distress.

Impression:
• Unilateral left-sided hearing loss with tinnitus – working diagnosis:  
  1. Cerumen impaction (most likely; common, reversible; clinician plans otoscopy).  
  2. Other causes to consider if ear canal clear: Menière’s disease, serous otitis media/Eustachian-tube dysfunction, acoustic neuroma (per DDx ranking).  
• Tinnitus acknowledged and patient advised of educational resources.

Plan:
• Arrange face-to-face clinic visit within 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to assess for wax or other external/middle-ear pathology.  
• Provide patient with tinnitus information leaflet link for education before visit.  
• Admin team to contact patient for scheduling; support number given.  
• Safety-net: If symptoms worsen or new issues occur, patient to book another video appointment.  
• Follow-up: After in-person assessment; further management dependent on findings (e.g., wax removal or additional investigations/referral).

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements: Allergies, current medications, full past medical history, social history (noise exposure), vitals, physical exam findings, formal follow-up date.  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear but limited; lacked comprehensive history, review of systems, and objective data.
